opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it, and this is one of the things I find most satisfying about TensorLogic, is that you don't need a separate concept of memory operations at all. Memory is just tensors, and reading and writing are just tensor equations.

Think about what a memory lookup is. You have a key, and you want to retrieve the value associated with it. In a database, that's a join: you join your query with the table of key-value pairs and project out the value. In TensorLogic, a relation is a tensor, and a join is a tensor product with summation over the shared indices, which is essentially an Einstein summation. So a memory read is literally one equation: the retrieved value is the sum over keys of the match between query and key times the stored value.

Here's the interesting part. If the match is a hard Boolean, you get a symbolic lookup, exactly what you'd get in Datalog or Prolog. If you make it soft, say a dot product followed by a softmax, you get attention. Attention in a transformer is a memory read. It's a soft join. And once you see it that way, the supposed divide between symbolic memory and neural memory goes away. It's the same operation with a different nonlinearity, and you can move continuously between them, for instance with a temperature parameter. At zero temperature you're doing exact deductive retrieval; as you raise it you get analogical, similarity-based retrieval.

Writing is the same story. Storing something means updating a tensor, adding an outer product of a key and a value, which is basically how associative memories and fast-weight schemes have always worked. In logic terms, it's asserting a new fact. Same operation, two descriptions.

Why does that matter in practice? A few reasons. First, you can mix them. Some parts of your memory can be crisp, curated facts you want retrieved exactly, with no hallucination, and other parts learned embeddings where you want generalization, all in the same program. Second, because it's all tensor algebra, it runs efficiently on GPUs and it's differentiable end to end, so you can learn what to store and how to retrieve it. Third, you get transparency. When the system pulls something from memory you can see which facts were joined, which you can't easily do when memory is smeared across a giant set of weights.

And I think this addresses one of the real weaknesses of current LLMs. Their memory is either the context window, which is transient, or the weights, which are opaque and expensive to update. What you want is a structured, persistent, queryable memory that the reasoning machinery treats as a first-class object. In TensorLogic that comes for free, because the knowledge base and the neural network are written in the same language.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that in Tensor Logic there really isn't a separate notion of a memory operation. That's sort of the point. Memory, reasoning, learning, inference: they all come out of one construct, which is the tensor equation. An equation says that a tensor on the left-hand side is defined by a product of tensors on the right, summed over the indices that don't appear on the left. That's a join followed by a projection, which is exactly what a Datalog rule does, and it's also exactly what an einsum does. So "storing" a fact is just having a tensor with a one in some cell, and "retrieving" it is contracting against that tensor.

Think about what that buys you. In a symbolic system, memory is a knowledge base and you look things up by matching. In a neural network, memory is smeared across the weights and you retrieve it by doing a forward pass. People treat these as totally different kinds of thing, and then they bolt on memory modules, retrieval, external stores, all these ad hoc patches. In Tensor Logic they're the same operation. A relation like Parent(x, y) is a Boolean tensor. An embedding table is a real-valued tensor. Attention is a tensor equation where the query and the key get contracted and then you contract with the value. Reading from memory and inferring a new fact are literally the same line of code.

The other thing I'd emphasize is the role of the temperature. When you run the equations at zero temperature you get hard, discrete lookups, which is what you want for exact recall. At higher temperatures you get soft matching, so retrieval generalizes to similar keys, and you can learn the tensors by gradient descent. That continuum is where I think a lot of the interesting stuff lives. You get the reliability of a database when you need it and the flexibility of a neural network when you need that, without changing the language you're working in.

And of course all of this runs on GPUs directly, because at the bottom it's just tensor contractions. Nobody has to write a special memory kernel.

astra-6.text:
I think of memory as something you should be able to represent and manipulate within the same language as the rest of the computation. In a logical view, you have facts and rules, and a memory lookup is a query: what matches these conditions? In a tensor view, you represent those facts as entries in a tensor, and the query becomes an operation over that tensor.

The interesting connection is to attention. You have a query, you compare it with keys, and you retrieve the corresponding values. That’s a form of associative memory. With exact matching, it looks like a symbolic lookup; with graded matching, it looks like differentiable retrieval.

But reading is only part of the story. You also need to express writing, updating, and potentially forgetting. And you need to distinguish the description of those operations from their implementation. Representing memory logically as a tensor doesn’t mean you should materialize some enormous dense array. You want sparse representations, indexing, and efficient retrieval. The goal is a common language for these operations, while still allowing the implementation to exploit their structure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of memory operations as indexing operations. In a tensor, you give me an index and I give you the value stored there. In logic, you give me a query and I retrieve the facts that match it. Those are two ways of looking at essentially the same operation, and TensorLogic lets you express them in a common language.

The interesting thing is that the index doesn’t have to be a single, discrete address. It can be a distribution over addresses, so reading from memory becomes a weighted combination of the things stored there. That gives you a differentiable memory operation. Attention is a very natural example: you compare a query with keys, and those matches determine how you combine the values.

So you can move between exact retrieval and this softer, learned retrieval. You don’t have to build a separate conceptual apparatus for each one.
